Odd, i had the same problem in the 2R+F reports, either with v1.2 or

Regarding the new players, i do the following:
- go to "http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/"
- choose under "Prince Resources" the "Add a VEKN Member" option
- it will show the following message at the bottom "Next available
VEKN ID is XXXXXXX"
- I fill the boxes (ask players for a valid email address) and i
always place the players password equal to his/her Vekn ID, so if i
insert player 3120000, I will assign as his password, the 312000o
number
- if an error appears stating the email address is already in use, you
can always "mistype" the domain, i.e., "pla...@hotmail.com" changed to
"pla...@hotmail.pt" (I'm Portuguese so I use PT)
- you'll have the account created (though with a wrong email address)
- players must go to the WW page and create their own accounts
- after players get registed, they should go under "getting started"
and "associate <their> vekn ID"
- if they have any trouble doing it so, they should send and email to
"vtessupport(a)white-wolf.com" stating which is their Vekn ID and to
which account do they want to associate with.

Usually players have to send the email because the vekn ID association
does not retrieve the Vekn Member password inserted previously.

Messages.Author: librarian
Messages.Body:


Get 3x5 cards. Write everyone's name at the top - or have them do it.

Shuffle the cards.

Lay them out. Round 1, solved, easy. I write down each player's table
and position on the card at this time.

Round 2 - get everyone's card. Shuffle.

Lay them out again. If you hit a same pred/prey relationship, take that
card and move it to the bottom of the stack. If you get to the end, and
those two have the same pred/prey relationship in round 1, take the last
person and switch her with the first player you set down.

I also write down their round 2 positions at this time as well.

Simple, done. Sufficiently random.

best -

chris

Of course there is a 2R optimal seating. It's been generated quite often by hand
(since it's easy enough to do an optimal 2R by hand). For small participation
tournaments, creating the seating by hand will produce a better seating than
selecting two rounds from an optimal-for-three-rounds seating.

And creating the seating by hand is a good exercise for organizers (helping
develop the skills necessary to handle drops and adds, even in 3R+F tournaments).

That's odd. I just got The Archon out and set it up for 12 Methuselahs.
There's no such result in the round 2 seating chart I'm looking at.
Assuming the first round is setup like this:

A -> B -> C -> D (-> A)
E -> F -> G -> H (-> E)
I -> J -> K -> L (-> I)

...the second round looks like this:

K -> A -> H -> B (-> K)
C -> E -> L -> F (-> C)
G -> I -> D -> J (-> G)

So I'm not sure how that happened. In the above setup, three pairs
of players from the first set of tables are seated together on the
same table in the second round. (This is the minimum possible, I
think, given how few players there are.) A and B are allies, E and
F are allies, and I and J are allies in the second round. No pair
of players from the same table are predator/prey at all.

If anything, the only sub-optimal complaint I can think of is that
there's no chance of reversing a predator/prey relationship at all
using the tables, whereas with total randomization, there should
be a significant chance of it happening.

> I mean, not horribly critical or anything (although the vagaries of
> wacky 2R seating out of a system that was designed to work optimally for
> 3R certainly meant that Ben was totally hosed), but likely less optimal
> than, say, a pile of 12 index cards getting shuffled and dealt out.

At least, not the one I have.

I disagree. I think there's likely a decent chance would cause

> This is not to say that our stalwart tournament organizer James was
> remotely negligent--we didn't know that was gonna happen, and just went
> with it, but my experience with the Archon is that, in fact, it is sub
> optimal for seating a 2R+F tournament, and just a pile of index cards
> shuffled, dealt out (with illegal seating being noticed and aborted)
> tends to work much better.

Even if James had used The Archon, I still wouldn't agree with this.
I'll bet if you laid out index cards randomly (picking up and reshuffling
every time an "unacceptable layout" occurred; unacceptable layouts being
the repeat of predator/prey relationships), you'll find this happens
quite a lot. I haven't analyzed this to the nth degree, but I
wouldn't be at all surprised. In the best redistribution of players
possible from one round to the next, each table _must_ contain at least
one pair of players who were together at a table the previous round.
If any of these three pairs of players are seated predator/prey the same
way you seated then in the first round, you pick up cards and redeal. So
this leaves only three possibilities: they're allies, or their predator
prey relationship is reversed, or they were allies in the previous round
so it doesn't matter (a 1-in-3 chance for that pair). I don't think this
leaves a very high chance that you'd get no reversed pairs, considering
that you'll frequently get sub-optimal redistributions of players (aka
three or all four from the same table first round go to the same table
second round).

Fred

Sure. No chart is going to feature any degree of optimization if you
change the number of players between rounds. They can't. They weren't
planned for that purpose and preplanning is the whole point of using
a chart. If I have a drop between rounds, I expect I'll usually have
to give in and just seat the second round manually anyway.

> The issue of Player A and Player C in R1 becoming prey/predator in R2
> (i.e. my R1 grand prey becomes my predator in R2) is likely a fixed
> certainty in a +/-12 player event in the Archon at some point. Using
> manual randomization can result in this, but also can avoid this.

...or it can be even worse. Again, I have a feeling that if you worked
out the odds and analyzed this to the nth degree, you'd find that you
get more such problems on average from the random table than either of
these charts. The order of second round play in The Archon has never
looked bad to me in any of the times I've used it. But then, my belief
is that some of these sitatuatins (e.g. two allies at a table in a
12-player tournament winding up as predator and prey in the second
round) are a LOT harder to avoid than you seem to believe, at least
with smaller numbers of players to work with. (18 players, for
instance, should be a much different story.) That's probably the root
of our differences.

Fred
